Notes on shipping slowly

I have been building the same product for 3 years. In that time the team grew from 2 people to 11, and the release cadence went from weekly to roughly monthly. That sounds like failure. It was not.

The first version shipped in 2023 with an SQL backend, a single API server, and no tests. It served 12,000 requests a day and fell over twice a week. We spent 40% of every sprint on incidents [1].

What changed

We stopped measuring velocity and started measuring the time between a bug report and a fix in production. That number was 9 days. It is now 4-6 hours. The work that moved it was unglamorous: a test suite, a staging environment, and a rule that nobody merges on a Friday.

Speed is a lagging indicator of clarity.

The AWS bill went from $400 a month to $2.8K, then back down to $1.1K once we understood our own access patterns. Cf. the storage tiering work described at https://theslowbuild.example.com/tiering which took 3 weeks and paid for itself in 5 months.

What I would tell myself in 2023

Write the test. Ship the smaller thing. A 500 ms page load is not an emergency; a 30% error rate is. And do not let anyone tell you that a team of 2 people needs a Kubernetes cluster.

Thanks for reading The Slow Build.
